title.text: Can I trust this model? Overfitting, cross-validation and leakage

objects.text: How do we know a model that predicts motor winding temperature will still work on a motor it has never seen?

CML3111  |  Electrical, Mechatronics, Robotics and Communications  |  Week 10, class 3 of 4  |  Friday 20 November 2026, 11:00 to 14:00
KLAi  |  International University of East Africa  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. In the first two classes you built models that predict motor winding temperature and models that answer yes or no. Today we ask the question an engineer must always ask: can I trust this?

A score that looks good is not enough. We learn how a model fools us, and how to test it so that it cannot.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can
Explain underfitting, a good fit and overfitting (the bias-variance trade-off), and choose max_depth with a validation curve
Work out training error, validation error, the generalisation gap, and a cross-validation mean and standard deviation, by hand
Score a model with K-fold and GroupKFold cross-validation, and report the mean with its standard deviation
Name three kinds of data leakage and use a checklist that blocks them

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can explain underfitting, a good fit and overfitting, the bias-variance trade-off, and you can choose max_depth by looking at a validation curve. You can work out the training error, the validation error, the generalisation gap, and the mean and standard deviation of cross-validation scores, by hand.

You can score a model with K-fold and GroupKFold. And you can name three kinds of data leakage and keep a checklist that blocks them. Nothing is submitted today. At the end I explain how the class counts.

We have three hours. The first seventy minutes are concepts only, with no laptop, so you can listen and ask. Then a break. Then the lab, about an hour and a quarter, where you run everything on your own data. The ideas come first and the code comes second.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Why is a majority-class baseline (a model that always predicts no) a poor model, even when its accuracy is about 80 percent?
2.  In a confusion matrix, what is a false negative (FN) and what is a false positive (FP)?
3.  What happened to recall and false positives when we lowered the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Class 2. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Why is a majority-class baseline (a model that always predicts no) a poor model, even when its accuracy is about 80 percent? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. It finds none of the real positive cases, so its recall is 0. Accuracy hides that.

Question two. In a confusion matrix, what is a false negative (FN) and what is a false positive (FP)? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. False negative: the model said no (negative) and the truth was yes (positive). False positive: the model said yes and the truth was no.

Question three. What happened to recall and false positives when we lowered the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. Recall rose from 0.67 to 1.00. False positives stayed at 0.

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Class 2

rows.text: Why is a majority-class baseline (a model that always predicts no) a poor model, even when its accuracy is about 80 percent?
It finds none of the real positive cases, so its recall is 0. Accuracy hides that.
In a confusion matrix, what is a false negative (FN) and what is a false positive (FP)?
False negative: the model said no (negative) and the truth was yes (positive). False positive: the model said yes and the truth was no.
What happened to recall and false positives when we lowered the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3?
Recall rose from 0.67 to 1.00. False positives stayed at 0.

slides.notes:
Here are the answers, so you can check yourself and use this slide to revise. A majority-class baseline, a model that always predicts no, can have a high accuracy, but it finds no real positive case, so its recall is zero. A false negative is a no when the truth was yes, and a false positive is a yes when the truth was no.

Lowering the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 moved recall from 0.67 to 1.00 on the validation rows. Today we ask a different question about the same models: can we trust a score at all?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: The model fits the noise in the training set (it nearly memorises it) and does worse on new rows. Underfitting is the opposite: too simple to learn the pattern.
Scoring a model K times. The rows are cut into K parts called folds. Each fold takes one turn as the validation fold (held-out fold).
Information from outside the training set reaches the model while it is trained, so the score looks better than it really is.
Too simple a model misses the pattern (high bias, underfitting). Too flexible a model chases noise (high variance, overfitting).
A fixed number (random_state in scikit-learn) that makes a random choice repeat exactly.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Overfitting. The model fits the noise in the training set (it nearly memorises it) and does worse on new rows. Underfitting is the opposite: too simple to learn the pattern.

Cross-validation. Scoring a model K times. The rows are cut into K parts called folds. Each fold takes one turn as the validation fold (held-out fold).

Data leakage. Information from outside the training set reaches the model while it is trained, so the score looks better than it really is.

Bias-variance trade-off. Too simple a model misses the pattern (high bias, underfitting). Too flexible a model chases noise (high variance, overfitting).

Random seed. A fixed number (random_state in scikit-learn) that makes a random choice repeat exactly.

title.text:
A model that looks good on paper
can fail on a new machine or site

objects.text: A model is built from data on four motors and then used on a fifth motor at another site.
A winding temperature warning is based on the model’s prediction.
If the prediction is wrong, a winding burns or a motor stops when it did not need to.

slides.notes:
Start with a story from your own field. A model is built from data on four motors and then used on a fifth motor at another site. A winding temperature warning is based on the model’s prediction. If the prediction is wrong, a winding burns or a motor stops when it did not need to.

In the office the model looked excellent, so everybody trusted it. The trouble is that the office score came from rows the model had already been trained on, or from a test that was too easy. Today is about checking a model the way real life will check it.

Have you ever trusted a number from a machine or a spreadsheet and then been surprised?

title.text: A model must do well on rows it has never seen

objects.alt: A model must do well on rows it has never seen

objects.text: Generalisation means doing well on held-out data: rows the model has never seen.

runs.text: The tree was trained on the training set, so its error there is almost zero.
The validation set was held out. On it the prediction error is far larger. The difference is the generalisation gap.

slides.notes:
Here is one tree, grown ten questions deep, scored two ways. The training set is the rows it was trained on, and there its error is 0.00 deg C, which is almost perfect. The validation set was held out, and there its error is 3.95 deg C. The difference between the two is called the generalisation gap.

Same model, same data, two very different stories. Doing well on held-out rows it has never seen is called generalisation, and it is the only thing we really want. A score on rows the model was trained on tells us about its memory, and a score on new rows tells us about its skill.

Which score would you show a client?

title.text:
Underfitting, a good fit and
overfitting look like three students

objects.alt: Underfitting, a good fit and overfitting look like three students

objects.text: The marks in the picture are illustrative (made up). Each student stands for one kind of model.

runs.text: Practice paper = training set. New paper = held-out rows.
Bias-variance trade-off: too simple a model misses the pattern, too flexible a model chases noise.

slides.notes:
Think of three students. The first read nothing, so the practice paper and the new paper both go badly. That is underfitting: a model too simple to learn the pattern, which the industry calls high bias. The second understood the ideas, so the marks are good on both papers.

That is a good fit. The third memorised last year’s answers. Perfect on the practice paper and poor on the new paper. That is overfitting: the model fits the noise, which the industry calls high variance. Balancing the two is the bias-variance trade-off. The practice paper stands for the training set, the new paper for held-out rows, and the marks are made up.

Can you think of someone who passed by memory and then struggled on the job?

title.text:
Reminder from Class 1: MAE and
RMSE measure the prediction error

objects.alt: Reminder from Class 1: MAE and RMSE measure the prediction error

rows.text: The mean size of the error. The bars drop any minus sign
MSE: mean of the squared errors. RMSE: its square root, in the target unit
n rows scored; y is the actual target of row i; ŷ (y-hat) is the prediction
15 validation rows; motor winding temperature in deg C

objects.text: Illustrative example (made up): errors of 1, 2 and 3 give MAE = 2, MSE = 4.67 and RMSE = 2.16.

slides.notes:
Before we use the word MAE all class, here is a reminder from Class 1. For every row, take the actual target and the prediction, and look at the size of the prediction error. The MAE is the mean of those errors, and the bars mean we drop any minus sign.

The RMSE squares each error first, averages, and then takes the square root, so one big error counts for more. Our linear regression model from Class 1 had an MAE of 0.78 deg C and an RMSE of 0.92 deg C on the validation rows. Today we mostly use the MAE.

Why would one very large error matter more to an engineer?

title.text:
The validation curve: as max_depth grows, training
error keeps falling but validation error stops

objects.alt: The validation curve: as max_depth grows, training error keeps falling but validation error stops

objects.text: A validation curve plots both errors against model complexity, here max_depth (most questions a row is asked).

runs.text: Each dot is one tree. Black: training error, falling to 0.00. Red: validation error. Between them: the generalisation gap.
The gold band is the max_depth we choose.

slides.notes:
This is a validation curve from our data. It plots error against model complexity. Each point is a tree with a different max_depth, the largest number of questions a row can be asked on the way down the tree. The black line is the error on the training rows, and it falls all the way to 0.00.

The red line is the validation error. It falls at first and then stops improving, and at depth 10 it sits at 3.95. The distance between the lines is the generalisation gap. The gold band is the depth we choose, depth 7. At the end of the Class 1 lab you tried depths 1, 2 and 8.

This curve is what you were seeing. Where does the generalisation gap start to grow?

title.text:
Training error, validation error and the
generalisation gap are short formulas

objects.alt: Training error, validation error and the generalisation gap are short formulas

rows.text: Mean absolute error: the average size of the prediction error. The small label train or val says which rows
How many rows. The small label tr means training and va means validation
A row number. The sum adds up the rows of that group
The real target of row i, and the model’s prediction for it. The bars | | drop any minus sign
motor winding temperature and the tree’s answer, in deg C

slides.notes:
Class 1 gave you the MAE. Here it is again, written for two groups of rows. The training error adds up the size of the prediction error on every training row, then divides by the number of training rows. The validation error does the same on the validation rows.

The bars mean the size of the error, so a plus or a minus makes no difference. In our data at depth 10 the training error is 0.00 deg C and the validation error is 3.95 deg C. Which rows is the tree trained on, and which rows does it never see?

title.text:
The generalisation gap is the validation
error minus the training error

objects.alt: The generalisation gap is the validation error minus the training error

rows.text: Generalisation gap: how much worse the model is on new rows
Validation error, from the formula before
Training error, from the formula before

objects.text: A gap near 0 means about the same error on new rows as on the training set. A big gap means overfitting.

slides.notes:
The generalisation gap is one subtraction: the validation error minus the training error. At depth 10 it is 3.95 minus 0.00, which is 3.95 deg C. At our chosen depth, depth 7, it is 3.91 minus 0.12, which is 3.79 deg C. A small gap says the model does about as well on new rows as on its training set.

A big gap says it is overfitting, fitting the noise in the training set. Next we see the gap for five depths in one table.

title.text:
As max_depth grows, the training error keeps
falling but the validation error does not

objects.text: MAE in deg C. A leaf node is a final node at the bottom of the tree, and it holds the prediction. A deeper tree has more leaf nodes. The linear regression model from Class 1 scores 0.78 deg C, better than every tree.

slides.notes:
Same numbers as the curve, in a table. Look at the leaf nodes, the final nodes at the bottom of the tree. Every row ends in exactly one leaf node, and the tree gives every row in it the same prediction. At depth 1 there are 2 leaf nodes.

At depth 10 there are 58, for only 58 training rows, so the tree is close to keeping one answer for each row. That is overfitting. The last column is the generalisation gap from the last slide. One more fact for later: the linear regression model from Class 1 scored 0.78 deg C, better than every tree.

A deeper tree is not a better model. What does that suggest about the shape of this data?

title.text:
We choose max_depth on the validation
set and keep the test set sealed

objects.alt: We choose max_depth on the validation set and keep the test set sealed

objects.text: Each set is made of whole equipment groups. The picture shows how many rows each set has.

runs.text: There are only 15 validation rows, so a score can move by luck.
We never tune anything on the test set.

slides.notes:
How did we choose depth 7?

We looked at the validation set only. The picture shows the three sets of our data: the training set from groups E1 to E4, the validation set from group E5, and the test set from group E6. We never touch the test set today. And we must be honest about the validation set: it has only 15 rows, so its scores are noisy, and a change of a few percent could be luck.

So we need a rule for choosing a model that does not chase small differences. That rule comes next. Why would picking the lowest score alone be risky with so few rows?

title.text:
Choose the simplest model within
a tolerance of the best score

objects.alt: Choose the simplest model within a tolerance of the best score

rows.text: Validation MAE of the tree with max_depth d
The lowest validation MAE over depths 1 to 10
The tolerance limit: the lowest value plus 5 percent
The chosen depth: the smallest d that passes

objects.text: A rule of thumb (parsimony: prefer the simpler model), like the one-standard-error rule. d* = chosen max_depth.

slides.notes:
Here is the rule for choosing the simplest model within a tolerance of the best validation score, as arithmetic. Find the lowest validation error, V min. For us it is 3.84 deg C, at depth 9. Add 5 percent by multiplying by 1.05, which gives the limit, 4.03 deg C.

Any depth whose validation error is at or below the limit is within the tolerance of the best. The depths that pass are 7, 8, 9, 10. We take the smallest of them, depth 7, because a simpler tree is less likely to overfit. This is a common practical rule, the idea of parsimony, similar in spirit to the one-standard-error rule.

The 5 percent is our own choice and it is not a law. What would change if the limit were 1.00?

title.text:
One split can be lucky, so K-fold cross-validation
lets every fold take a turn as the validation fold

objects.alt: One split can be lucky, so K-fold cross-validation lets every fold take a turn as the validation fold

objects.text: K-fold cross-validation cuts the 58 training rows into K = 5 folds (parts of the rows), in the order the rows appear (no shuffle).

runs.text: In each row, the tree is trained on 4 folds and scored on the gold fold: the validation fold (held-out fold).
After 5 rows each fold has been the validation fold once. The 5 scores of a max_depth 4 tree are on the right.

slides.notes:
A single validation split is one test on one day, and the day may be lucky or unlucky. K-fold cross-validation takes several tests. Cut the 58 training rows into five folds. In the first row of the picture, the tree is trained on folds two to five, and fold one is the validation fold, also called the held-out fold.

It is used only to score the tree. Some books call it the test fold, but it is not the sealed test set E6. In the next row a different fold is the validation fold, and so on, until every fold has had its turn. Here are the five scores for a depth-4 tree, from 3.95 to 4.82 deg C. Five scores tell us more than one.

title.text:
K-fold gives k scores, and we report
their mean and their standard deviation

objects.alt: K-fold gives k scores, and we report their mean and their standard deviation

rows.text: The MAE when fold j is the validation fold (j is the fold number)
The number of folds, so the number of scores
The mean (average) of the k scores (s with a bar)
The standard deviation (sigma): the typical distance of a score from the mean. We divide by k, as np.std does

slides.notes:
Two formulas turn the five scores into two numbers. The mean adds up the k scores and divides by k. The standard deviation asks how far each score sits from the average, squares those distances so plus and minus cannot cancel, takes their average, and then the square root.

For our five scores the mean is 4.45 deg C and the standard deviation is 0.33 deg C. We divide by k, the same as NumPy, so your numbers match the notebook. A small standard deviation means the folds agree. A large one means the score depends on which fold you ask. First we do it by hand with four easy numbers.

title.text:
By hand with four illustrative scores: the
mean is 3 and the standard deviation is 0.71

objects.text: Mean = (2 + 3 + 3 + 4) / 4 = 3. Mean of the squared distances = (1 + 0 + 0 + 1) / 4 = 0.5 (the variance). The square root of 0.5 is 0.71, the standard deviation. These four scores are illustrative (made up).

slides.notes:
Let us do it by hand with four illustrative, made-up fold scores: two, three, three and four. The mean is twelve divided by four, which is three. Now the standard deviation. How far is each score from the mean?

Minus one, zero, zero and plus one. Square them, so that plus and minus cannot cancel: one, zero, zero, one. Their mean is a half, which is the variance. The square root of a half is 0.71. That number is the standard deviation, the typical distance of a fold score from the mean. Check the 0.71 on your own page.

title.text:
The same steps on our five real scores:
mean 4.45, standard deviation 0.33 deg C

objects.text: Mean = 22.24 / 5 = 4.45. Mean of squares = 0.543 / 5 = 0.109. Square root = 0.33, the standard deviation. Worked from unrounded scores, so the last digit can differ.

slides.notes:
Now the same steps on the five real scores from our depth-4 tree. The scores add up to 22.24, so the mean is 4.45 deg C. Each score has a distance from that mean, some above and some below, and the distances add up to zero. We square them, and the squares add up to 0.543.

Divide by five to get 0.109, and the square root of that is 0.33 deg C. That is the standard deviation you will see in the notebook. Compare it with the mean. Is it small or large?

title.text:
GroupKFold holds out a whole equipment group
in each fold, which is how the model is really used

objects.alt: GroupKFold holds out a whole equipment group in each fold, which is how the model is really used

objects.text: GroupKFold keeps each equipment group whole. In each fold one group, E1, E2, E3 or E4, is the validation fold.

runs.text: The tree is trained on the other three groups and scored on the held-out motor group, like a new site.
Each fold gives one score. The mean and standard deviation are worked out as before.

slides.notes:
Plain K-fold mixes rows from every group, so the model has already seen the same motor while it is trained. In real use a new motor arrives, and nobody has seen it. GroupKFold fixes that by keeping each equipment group whole. In each fold it holds out one group, E1, E2, E3 or E4, trains on the other three, and scores the held-out group.

The four scores run from 3.67 to 5.08 deg C, with a mean of 4.15. Which of the two designs looks more like the situation you will face at work?

title.text:
GroupKFold uses the same formulas,
with equipment groups as the folds

objects.alt: GroupKFold uses the same formulas, with equipment groups as the folds

rows.text: The group held out in one fold: E1, E2, E3 or E4
E1, then E2, E3, E4 in turn
Number of rows in group g (the small label g)
MAE on group g (the small label g), using a tree that was never trained on g
Mean of the 4 scores, and their standard deviation

slides.notes:
GroupKFold needs no new maths. The score for a group g is the MAE on the rows of that group, using a tree trained on the other three groups that never saw g. Then we take the mean of the four scores and their standard deviation, with the same two formulas as before, with four in place of k.

Our four scores have a mean of 4.15 deg C and a standard deviation of 0.56 deg C. Which group was hardest to predict?

title.text:
The same max_depth 4 tree gets three
different scores, depending on how we test it

rows.text: K-fold, k = 5 (rows in order, no shuffle)

objects.text: MAE in deg C. Group E5 turned out harder than the average group, so its single score is higher than both averages. The standard deviation shows how far to trust each mean.

slides.notes:
Here is the same tree scored three ways. The single split on group E5 says 4.79. Plain K-fold says 4.45, with a standard deviation of 0.33. GroupKFold says 4.15, with a standard deviation of 0.56. Group E5 happened to be harder than the average group, so the single split gave a gloomier answer than cross-validation.

It could just as easily have been luckier. Report the mean and the standard deviation, and say how the folds were made. Which of the three would you quote to a client, and what would you add?

title.text:
Data leakage is information from outside
the training set reaching the model

objects.alt: Data leakage is information from outside the training set reaching the model

objects.text: Data leakage: information from held-out data, which the model should not see, reaches the model while it is trained.

runs.text: Held-out rows are the validation or test rows. The dashed red arrow is the leakage.
The score looks excellent, then the model fails on real new rows.

slides.notes:
Now the second big danger. Data leakage means information from outside the training set reaches the model while it is trained. The picture shows the normal path along the bottom: the training rows train the model, and then the model gets a score. The held-out rows are the validation or test rows, and they must stay out of training.

If anything from them slips in, along the red arrow, the model has seen the answers. The score then looks excellent, and the first real machine breaks the spell. The worst part is that nothing warns you. There is no error message, only a score that is too good.

Have you seen a result that looked too good to be true?

title.text: Data leakage comes in three common kinds

objects.alt: Data leakage comes in three common kinds

objects.text: All three make the score look too good.

slides.notes:
Three kinds cover most cases. Train-test contamination: validation rows end up in the training set, for example by joining two files, or by tuning on the test rows again and again. Preprocessing leakage: an imputer, which fills missing values, or a scaler, which rescales columns to a common scale, is fitted on all rows before the split, so the training set carries information about the validation rows.

Target leakage: a feature is computed from the target, such as a column that is only filled in after the failure has happened. We show each one with real numbers.

title.text:
Train-test contamination: validation rows in
the training set make the score look perfect

objects.alt: Train-test contamination: validation rows in the training set make the score look perfect

objects.text: Same max_depth 10 tree. Only the training set changed.

runs.text: In the leaky run the tree was already trained on the validation rows, so it reproduces their answers (overfitting).
The honest score is the real one.

slides.notes:
This is the real demonstration from our data. The same tree, depth ten. In the honest version the validation rows are held out, and the validation error is 3.95 deg C. In the leaky version we put the validation rows into the training set first, which is train-test contamination.

The error drops to 0.00. The tree has simply memorised those rows, so the leaky score is perfect and tells us nothing. Nobody would do this on purpose, but a join or a copy and paste can do it quietly. Which of the two scores would predict a new machine?

title.text:
A Pipeline fits the imputer on the training set
only, which prevents preprocessing leakage

objects.alt: A Pipeline fits the imputer on the training set only, which prevents preprocessing leakage

objects.text: Median of ambient_c: 26.07 from the training set, 25.37 from all rows (preprocessing leakage). Only one value is missing, so the score did not change.

slides.notes:
Preprocessing leakage is the quiet one. If you fill missing values, or scale columns, using all the rows, the validation rows have helped to decide the fill. In our data the median ambient temperature is 26.07 from the training set and 25.37 from all rows. We tried both, and the validation error did not change, because only one value is missing.

So here the habit costs nothing. That is exactly why it is dangerous: a clean score does not prove a clean method. The fix is a Pipeline, which chains the imputer and the tree. In every fold it fits the imputer on the training folds only, then fills the validation fold with those same numbers.

title.text:
The pipeline rule: fit on the training
set only, then apply the same numbers

objects.alt: The pipeline rule: fit on the training set only, then apply the same numbers

rows.text: i is the row, j the column, x the value in row i and column j, n the number of training rows. In preprocessing leakage, i includes validation rows
Median of column j over the training rows
Mean and standard deviation of column j over the training rows
The z-score (scaled value) of row i in column j

slides.notes:
Here is the pipeline rule as a formula. The median for column j is taken over the training rows only. The mean and the standard deviation for column j are also taken over the training rows only. Then the same three numbers are applied to every row, including the validation rows.

The leakage is simple to state: if the row number i also runs over the validation rows, the imputer or scaler has seen them. Take row one of our training data. Its load is 59.15. Subtract the mean 59.89, divide by the standard deviation 22.73, and the z-score is -0.03.

Class 2 used this scaler, and the pipeline does it for you inside every fold.

title.text:
Target leakage: a feature built from the target
gives a great score that cannot be repeated

objects.alt: Target leakage: a feature built from the target gives a great score that cannot be repeated

objects.text: With that feature a max_depth 4 tree scores 1.09 deg C. With honest features it scores 4.79 deg C.

runs.text: target_rounded is the target rounded to a whole number. At prediction time the target is unknown.
A feature recorded after the event is also target leakage.

slides.notes:
This is target leakage. Suppose someone adds a feature that is the target rounded to a whole number. A depth-4 tree with that feature scores 1.09 deg C on the validation rows, against 4.79 without it. It looks like a miracle. But when a new reading arrives, the target is exactly what we do not know yet, so the feature cannot be filled in.

Real examples are a repair code written after the failure, or a daily total computed from the very value we predict. Ask of every feature: will I have this at the moment I need the prediction?

title.text:
Keep this checklist: five questions
before you trust a score

objects.text: Was the score measured on held-out data (rows the model never saw)?
Were the imputer and the scaler fitted on the training set only (no preprocessing leakage)?
Does any feature come from the target, or only exist after the event (target leakage)?
Is the test set (group E6) still sealed?
Is the score a cross-validation mean, shown with its standard deviation?

slides.notes:
Here is the checklist I want you to keep, and I will ask for it again next class. One: was the score measured on held-out data, rows the model never saw?

Two: were the imputer and the scaler fitted on the training set only?

Three: does any feature come from the target, or only exist after the event?

Four: is the test set, group E6, still sealed?

Five: is the score a cross-validation mean, shown with its standard deviation?

If you can answer yes to all five, you may trust the number a little. If you cannot, find out why before you show it to anyone. Take a photo of this slide now.

title.text:
The same code can give different numbers, so we fix
the random seed (random_state) and write it down

objects.text: MAE in deg C. The data and the code are the same in every row. Only the seed changed. A random seed makes a random choice repeat exactly. Your last digit can differ.

slides.notes:
Random choices sit inside many tools. A tree breaks ties at random, and shuffled folds mix the rows at random. A random seed, which scikit-learn calls random_state, is a number that makes those choices repeat exactly. Look at the table. With the same data and the same code, the depth-10 tree scores about 4.7, 3.9 or 3.8 deg C, depending on the seed.

So a number without its random seed is only half a result. We use random_state equal to seventeen everywhere, and the difference between seeds also tells us how much of a score is luck. Why does a colleague need your seed?

Reproducibility means that someone else, or you in six months, can run the same code and get the same numbers. For that you need a short record. Which data file, and how many rows. After cleaning in Class 1, the usable rows are fewer than the rows in the file, and the record says so.

How the rows were split. The random seed. And the versions of Python, NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn, because a new version can change a result slightly. The notebook prints this record in the last step. Paste it under every result you report. It takes ten seconds. It is the difference between a result and a claim.

title.text: Trust comes from four habits

objects.text: Next class: features and choosing a model. These habits are the rulebook.

slides.notes:
Let us gather it up in four habits. Score on rows the model never saw. Use cross-validation, so you report a mean with a standard deviation, and GroupKFold when the model will meet new machines. Fit every preprocessing step, the imputer and the scaler, on the training set only.

And keep a record for reproducibility: the random seed, the data file and the versions. With these four habits, a score becomes something you can defend. Before the break, say aloud which habit you are most likely to forget.

title.text: Read the workflow before you write it

runs.text: pipeline = make_pipeline(imputer, tree_model)
group_kfold = GroupKFold(n_splits=4)
cv_scores = cross_val_score(
pipeline, X_train, y_train,
groups=groups, cv=group_kfold,
scoring=
"neg_mean_absolute_error"
print(-cv_scores.mean(), cv_scores.std())

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: make_pipeline chains the imputer and the tree into one model (a Pipeline).
GroupKFold(n_splits=4) makes 4 folds. Each fold holds out one equipment group as the validation fold.
cross_val_score runs the whole pipeline on every fold and returns one score per fold.
The scoring name gives the MAE with a minus sign, so we print -cv_scores.mean().
cv_scores.std() is the standard deviation of the scores.

slides.notes:
Before the break, here is the workflow in six lines. First the Pipeline: the imputer and the tree, chained into one model, so the imputer is fitted inside every fold. Then GroupKFold with four splits, so each fold holds out one equipment group, and we pass the group labels with groups.

Then cross_val_score, which runs that pipeline on every fold and returns one score per fold. The scoring name has the word neg in it, because scikit-learn likes bigger to be better, so errors come back negative. We put a minus in front to get the MAE back. Finally we print the mean and the standard deviation.

You can read this aloud now. In the lab you run it.
